text: The Pleasant Stay hotel case involved Jayalalithaa, the former Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu during 1991–1996, and her colleagues V. R. Nedunchezhiyan and T. M. Selvaganapathy, who were charged with misusing their office to allow Rakesh Mittal’s Pleasant Stay Hotel in Kodaikanal to build seven floors, violating development norms. In April 1991, Mittal was permitted to construct two floors; in January 1992, he sought approval for seven floors, which was rejected by the Kodaikanal township, prompting an appeal. He began constructing four floors without permission. On 13 May 1994, the Jayalalithaa government passed Government Order (G.O.) Ms. No.126, permitting five extra floors for a total of seven, against the norms. The order was passed by Jayalalithaa, Selvaganapathy, and water supply secretary H.M. Pandey, despite the Architectural and Aesthetics Aspects Committee (AAAC)’s recommendation against it. A subsequent G.O. Ms. No.317, effective from 13 May 1994, exempted the building from Development Control Rules. On 31 March 1994, the Madras High Court had ordered Mittal to use only the zero and first floors, an order later quashed along with the May 1994 G.O. The Palani Hills Conservation Council (PHCC) obtained a stay from the Madras High Court in December 1997 and won the legal battle. The trial, presided over by special judge Radhakrishnan in Chennai, was conducted by special public prosecutors N. Natarajan, S. Ramasamy, K.E. Venkataraman, R. Karunakaran, and advocate Sunder Mohan. The judge noted the First Investigation Report (FIR) was filed two years after the incident and that while there was a pecuniary advantage to the hotel management, no direct proof linked the government orders to personal gain for officials. Pandey, who knew the case details, did not pass the file directly to Jayalalithaa via Selvaganapathy. On 2 February 2000, the five accused—Jayalalithaa, Selvaganapathy, Pandey, Rakesh Mittal, and Palai N. Shanmugham—were convicted of criminal conspiracy and criminal misconduct by public servants; Jayalalithaa was sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment and fined ₹2,000, with the judge stating there was sufficient circumstantial evidence proving their involvement. On 9 February 2000, the Madras High Court suspended the sentence on appeal. The verdict triggered statewide protests and violence, including the burning of five buses, damage to fifty buses, and injuries to 40 people. In Dharmapuri, on 2 February 2000, three girls—Hemalatha, V. Gayathri, and Kokilavani—were burnt alive when a petrol bomb was thrown during a study tour return trip, with 16 others injured; the incident was broadcast on Sun TV and led to student protests and school closures. Two AIADMK cadres committed suicide by setting themselves on fire. The DMK accused AIADMK of inciting the violence, while AIADMK demanded a CBI probe, alleging DMK-supported Sun TV was present during the incident. The three AIADMK men convicted in the Dharmapuri incident were sentenced to death on 5 December 2007, later commuted to life imprisonment. Twenty-five other AIADMK cadres were convicted on lesser charges and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. The verdict occurred during a period when the Tamil Maanila Congress, allied with DMK in the 1996 elections, supported AIADMK in upcoming by-elections. Jayalalithaa was disqualified from contesting the 2001 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election due to the conviction, and the Supreme Court disqualified her on 21 September 2001, ruling that a convicted person cannot hold office of Chief Minister, despite claims of popular mandate. The governor of Tamil Nadu, Fathima Beevi, who administered the oath, was advised to step down by the Union Ministry, which submitted the report to the President of India; it was a rare instance of a constitutional functionary being removed for omission of duties. She resigned on 1 July 2001, and C. Rangarajan, then governor of Andhra Pradesh, was appointed as the acting governor. Following her disqualification, no clear successor emerged, and at an AIADMK meeting, O. Panneerselvam was chosen as Chief Minister. On 4 December 2001, the Madras High Court acquitted Jayalalithaa and four others of all charges in both the Pleasant Stay hotel and TANSI land acquisition cases. She contested and won the Andipatti assembly by-election in March 2002 and was sworn in as Chief Minister again. The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal on 24 November 2003, citing lack of legal evidence despite strong suspicion, and ordered that she "must atone her conscience in the whole controversy." It was later reported that she returned the land to the agency at a throwaway price.
